speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: REPORT ON PARIS MEETING OF MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I notice that there have been some questions asked in the house during my absence concerning the recent ministerial meeting of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization which was held in Paris on the 16th, 17th and 18th. I have made arrangements for copies of the communique which was issued to be distributed to the members of the house, but I am not sure whether or not they have been made available as yet. I also have copies in English and in French which I should like to table if that meets with the wishes of the house.
These meetings, by the way, were attended by the Minister of National Defence and myself. In the ordinary course the Minister of Finance would have been there as well, but he had to return to Ottawa after the meeting setting up the new organization known as O.E.C.D.
There was in the first place a review of the international situation and that went over the whole international picture, having to do primarily with the situation in the Soviet bloc and with Russian policy. Canada advocated that the NATO countries should have a flexibility in their reaction to statements and proposals made by the Soviet union. We do not think it is wise to be too rigid in the reaction to these various Soviet proposals. There was, of course, continued concern with regard to the situation in Berlin. As hon. members will notice, in the communique there was a paragraph which reads as follows:
The council regretted the lack of progress on the reunification of Germany on the basis of selfdetermination. With regard to Berlin, the council
reaffirmed their declaration of December 16, 1958. In face of the recent Soviet threats and harassing tactics, they once again declared their determination to protect the freedom of the people of West Berlin.
In the communique there was also a significant paragraph concerning disarmament. It is paragraph No. 4 and reads as follows:
The council deplored the lack of progress during the past year on disarmament, resulting from the communist states' withdrawal from the ten-power conference before even examining the western proposals. The council reaffirmed their support for the principles expressed in those proposals as a basis for attaining their common objective of general and complete disarmament by stages under effective international control. They expressed their hope for the early resumption of negotiations.
Then there was also a reference which will be found in paragraph 6 and also in paragraph 8 which, among other things, dealt with the question of the balance of nuclear and conventional weapons. In it there is this significant sentence:
There must be a proper balance in the forces of the alliance of nuclear and conventional strength to provide the required flexibility.
The basis for that sentence is that there is concern for fear the members of the alliance overlook the need of keeping up conventional arms. The worry is that the forces of NATO will be allowed to deteriorate or to depreciate in the field of conventional arms.
Then there were also two proposals made by the United States. They will be found in paragraph 7 of the communique. I will read the second part of this paragraph first:
The council welcomed the assurance of the United States to maintain in the NATO area United States nuclear weapons made available to NATO.
Some of the European nations have been afraid that the United States might withdraw a portion of their nuclear weapons already in Europe. This matter is viewed with some concern, so assurance was given by Secretary of State Herter to the effect that these nuclear weapons would be maintained in the European area of NATO.
In addition, Mr. Herter suggested the concept of a medium range ballistic missile multilateral force for consideration by the alliance. This was not put in the way of an actual proposal, but as a suggested concept. He did not want to be committed to any actual proposal because of course there is to be a change in the administration of the United States next month, and the present administration could not bind the incoming administration. In addition to that, congressional action would be required for a

Report on Paris NATO Meeting change in the law of the United States if this plan is to be carried out. Therefore, as I say, it was put forward as a concept.
Involved with that there was also a similar concept, that the United States might move five Polaris submarines to European waters. I think these would become part of the United States NATO fleet; like the sixth fleet in the Mediterranean.
These concepts were noted by other members of the council and instructions were given to the permanent representatives to study the suggestions and all related matters. Of course they would also have to be reviewed very carefully by the various governments because they involve serious and complicated questions; for example, the question of control of the medium range ballistic missiles if they should come under NATO. The MRBM multilateral force would also involve expenditures by the other countries which would have to provide the funds for these ballistic missiles.
Then there was a discussion on long term planning for NATO and various questions were considered; for example, consultation. There was no difficulty about consultation on matters having to do with the NATO area directly, but there was some difference of opinion concerning consultation on matters, for example, in Africa or in the Far East, which areas of course are not included in the NATO area.
Canada's opinion is that nations should be informed of the views of the other members of the alliance with regard to problems arising in these areas, but we have never agreed that there should be consultation in the sense of creating an obligation on the member countries with regard to areas outside the NATO area.
There was also the question of how the NATO countries should act in the United Nations. I think the secretary general would like to see NATO move as a bloc in the United Nations, but we pointed out that the only real bloc of that type in the world today is the Soviet bloc, based on dictatorship, so they can very easily move as a unit. The whole foundation of the other countries, the NATO countries, is based on democracy, on people being able to express their individual opinions and having nations express their individual opinions. We do not think it makes much sense to have a NATO bloc in the United Nations.
We also feel that some of the NATO countries have been rather downgrading the United Nations and taking this position: "Oh, well, after all we do not care what happens in the United Nations; we will not be bothered with it". Canada is convinced that is the wrong attitude.

maintopic: REPORT ON PARIS MEETING OF MINISTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: REPORT ON PARIS MEETING OF MINISTERS
speechtext:
There are now 99 nations in the United Nations. There are only nine in the Soviet bloc; there are 15 in NATO including West Germany which is not a member of the United Nations. That adds up to the necessity for winning friends in the United Nations. You cannot line up people any more down there; you have to have a case that will win the support of the noncommitted countries.
We believe that if the NATO nations came into the United Nations for that purpose, that is, the purpose of getting across our ideas and really worked at getting up resolutions which embarrass the Soviet side-we are not very good at it, though they are-I think if the NATO nations really put their backs into doing the job required at the United Nations under present conditions, very beneficial results would follow. We had quite an interesting discussion on that point.
Then there were various economic questions. It was felt that the main scope of NATO in the economic field at the present time is in connection with communist moves in the trade and economic field; that NATO should be a watchdog keeping track of what is done by the Soviet countries in this particular field and trying to devise measures to meet an offensive of that kind. As for the actual trading arrangements, we now believe that O.E.C.D. meet that requirement.
There is also great concern in NATO with regard to Greece and Turkey. They are underdeveloped countries, and they feel they should have help from other NATO countries. Their position met with a great deal of sympathetic understanding.
There was also discussion about holding a meeting of heads of state. Canada has felt -and our own Prime Minister has expressed this feeling on more than one occasion- that there is a need now, in the New Year, for the heads of government to come together and review the whole NATO picture. We are living in a different world today than we were ten years ago, and Canada is very anxious that there should be a meeting of the heads of governments. We got support for this from West Germany and Greece, but ran into the complication that the present United States administration cannot bind the new administration. Also, there is the fact that there are several very important conferences which the new president must attend early in the year. Thus no definite arrangement was made about a meeting of heads of government, but we are at liberty to raise the matter in the council should the international situation change before the ministerial meeting which is to be held in Oslo,

Norway early in May. Incidentally, Canada invited the other NATO nations to hold this meeting of heads of government in Canada. So that particular question remains unsettled at the moment.
In conclusion, may I say that the liveliness of the discussions demonstrated again the vitality of the alliance. There really is a great depth of understanding and friendship among the representatives of these 15 countries who meet twice a year. Down through the years there has developed a very remarkable spirit of co-operation, and we continue to believe that NATO has a great part to play in the affairs of the world. Canada has done her full share in the growth of this spirit, and I am sure there can be no question but that she will continue to do that in the years that lie ahead.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: REPORT ON PARIS MEETING OF MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin my few remarks by welcoming back from Paris the minister and his colleagues. We know they must have had a busy time in Paris and that they did everything that could be done there to contribute to the success and achievement of the NATO council meeting. It seems from the minister's statement and from what we have been able to read in the press that the discussions in Paris were frank, as they should be among friends. It also appears that, because of circumstances which have something to do with the United States political situation, it was not possible for the council, apart from other difficulties, to reach decisions in a way that might have been possible in different circumstances. I suppose it is not unfair to call this NATO council meeting a marking time meeting. Yet it is becoming clear that very soon some essential decisions will have to be taken in regard to the functioning of the NATO alliance.
I note in the communique, for instance- and the minister has already referred to this -three paragraphs dealing with the use by NATO members of nuclear weapons. Indeed, paragraph No. 6 to which the minister referred includes this sentence:
There must be a proper balance in the forces of the alliance of nuclear and conventional strength-
It is clear, because the decision was made a good many years ago, that the NATO forces are being trained at the present time in the use of nuclear tactical defensive weapons; therefore important decisions will soon have to be made by NATO itself, as they will have to be made by all the members of NATO as to individual national responsibility for the using or refusing to use weapons of this kind and as to the conditions, if they are to be used, under which they should be used.
Report on Paris NATO Meeting
It is interesting to note-and the minister also referred to this-that at least a suggestion, if not a proposal, has been made by the United States delegate which deals with the collective use by NATO of nuclear weapons. The minister also pointed out that there were some discussions of ways and means of strengthening political and economic consultation. That subject has been under discussion at every NATO council meeting from the day NATO was formed. This communique says, as so many communiques have said in the past, that the council studied once again ways and means of achieving better political consultation.
I do not think the problem is in achieving ways and means of doing this. The problem is developing the will to bring about better political consultation so that the interests of the members can be reconciled.
I think the minister is right indeed when he points out the undesirability of the NATO members trying to act as a bloc at the United Nations or anywhere else. I think the hon. gentleman was also wise in pointing out, as I gather he did in Paris, that while all the member nations have obligations to the alliance, we also have a pre-eminent obligation to the world organization of the United Nations. It should be a cardinal principle of policy of all the NATO members to reconcile those two obligations in a way which will not downgrade the world organization.
I believe the minister should have the support of every hon. member in the house in the effort he is making toward that end. At the same time I am sure the minister will agree with me when I say it is particularly important at the present time that the United Nations should not downgrade itself either by its actions or by its obstruction in the way of good actions. This is one of the major problems of foreign policy that confront every member of the United Nations at this time.
I note the minister's reference to the proposal for a summit meeting. There are occasions in NATO and outside NATO when summit meetings can be useful. Indeed, I suppose on some occasions they are essential. But I think we should take care before we support a meeting at the summit because, as the experience of the last year has shown, that kind of meeting, with all the publicity that attaches to it and all the expectations that are aroused by it, sometimes ends in disillusionment rather than constructive achievement. If a summit meeting is to be called to review, in the words of the minister, the whole picture, to review NATO and it workings, I suggest that kind of review should be taking place every week through the permanent council of NATO. Perhaps one of the most important things that could be

No doubt we will have an opportunity after the new year to debate international affairs generally, including NATO. Meanwhile, all I wish to say is that we on this side support the minister and his colleagues in every step they may take at NATO and at the United Nations in order that Canada can continue to play an effective part in the search for international peace and security.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this group joins with the Leader of the Opposition in welcoming the minister back to the house. I want to assure him that we miss him when he is absent, and we follow his sayings and his doings very closely from day to day. I also wish to thank him for providing us with a copy of the final communique of the ministerial conference of NATO just prior to making his brief report on his trip.
I must say, too, on behalf of this group that we were very pleased to note his reference to the relationship of NATO to the United Nations and his opposition to any attempt on the part of NATO countries to act as a bloc within the United Nations. I think he is on very sound ground in that respect. However, in reading the communique I note that the second section of paragraph 7 contains these words:
The council welcomed the assurance of the United States to maintain in the NATO area United States nuclear weapons made available to NATO.
I say without any equivocation that this group is opposed to the arming of NATO with nuclear weapons and the arming of other countries with nuclear weapons as well. In that connection I want to bring to the minister's attention the fact that recently I had the honour to be a member of the Canadian delegation to the interparliamentary union conference held in Tokyo. On the first day of general debate during that conference, I believe, the Polish delegate made a slashing attack upon the West German government and expressed very normal fears with respect to nuclear weapons and the possibility and danger of Polish territory being taken over in the days ahead.
What interested me and a number of other members of the commonwealth section of the delegation was the reply of the West German delegate who, when he spoke, replied in very moderate terms. He assured the conference that no nuclear weapons would ever be used by the German government without the consent of the president of the United States. At the time the comment was made it made me shudder, and we in this group are very


concerned about that situation, as are an increasing number of Canadians who are expressing the same concern with respect to the arming of other countries with nuclear weapons and the arming of NATO with such weapons.
Also, in paragraph 12 of the final communique we read the following:
In the economic field, they welcomed the creation of the O.E.C.D. which, by promoting balanced economic growth and the expansion of world trade, will benefit all the nations of the free world.
I quote that simply to bring to the attention of the house that the formation of O.E.C.D. illustrates quite clearly the complete failure to give effect to article II of the North Atlantic treaty itself.
I have made a few comments on behalf of this group, and when the debate on external affairs takes place early in the new year we will have an opportunity to express the policy of the C.C.F. on external affairs generally and particularly with respect to NATO.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secreiary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with leave of the house I have another statement to make in connection with the Canadian resolution on disarmament at the United Nations. When the communist five walked out of the ten-nation disarmament committee on June 27 of this year we decided that Canada should take some steps to try to bring about a resumption of negotiations as quickly as possible. One way of doing this, we thought, was to focus world opinion on the nuclear powers, thus bringing home to them very clearly the insistence of the peoples of all other countries of the world that active steps should be continued not only to bring about disarmament but to prevent the nuclear weapons race from continuing.
At the same time we decided to endeavour to emphasize the rights and the responsibilities in the disarmament field of the middle and smaller powers. After all, the people of the middle and smaller powers are either going to be bombed or killed by radiation as well as the people of the nuclear powers, and they have a right to make their wishes heard. In addition, they have the responsibility to do something about the question of disarmament. We do not believe that they can sit back and leave it wholly to the nuclear powers to work out a solution.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, we took action accordingly in the disarmament commission of the United Nations, and were successful in getting a resolution adopted unanimously

by that commission on August 18 which called, among other things, for the earliest possible continuation of disarmament negotiations.
Then the battle moved to the general assembly of the United Nations, and there we brought in a resolution, co-sponsored by Norway and Sweden, which would have provided for the appointment of a neutral chairman in the disarmament talks. We had in mind possibly a citizen of Switzerland. It would also have provided for an ad hoc committee of non-nuclear powers whose job would be to try to keep pressure on the powers to bring about a resumption of negotiations and then keep an eye on the negotiating committee once negotiations had been resumed. At this point I should like to praise Norway and Sweden for the part they have taken in this effort. In most cases the Scandinavian countries arrive at the same conclusions that Canada does, and the way in which we naturally seem to end up on the same side is remarkable.
We ran into certain obstacles. None of the nuclear powers were very enthusiastic about our resolution, which can be understood. We did not expect them to be singing hallelujahs in support of it. In addition, however, there is fairly widespread reluctance in the United Nations on the part of the middle and smaller powers to antagonizing any of the big fellows. Some do not want to antagonize the Soviet; others do not want to antagonize the western side. In any event, we finally amended our resolution so that it at least got the support of some of the western nuclear powers, and we also managed to get 18 co-sponsors from countries all over the world except Africa. We had no co-sponsor from Africa.
Our resolution on disarmament was only one of about 13. There has been discussion, off and on, in the first committee on these various disarmament resolutions. Finally it came to the time when the assembly was about to adjourn and, like the House of Commons here, there developed a great enthusiasm for rushing things through and getting rid of any contentious issues. We all know how that happens here in Ottawa, and there was the same reaction in New York.
There was quite strong sentiment in favour of deferring all these bothersome disarmament resolutions until the United Nations reconvenes on March 7. We have been worrying about this; it has been our biggest obstacle. Yesterday my parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), who is the vice chairman of the Canadian delegation and who, I may add, has been doing an outstanding job at the United Nations both this year and last year as well as two years earlier, I understand, when he was acting in the same capacity, 90205-6-62
Statement on Disarmament Resolution moved a procedural resolution which would have had the effect of bringing about a vote at once on two resolutions, the one advocating no further nuclear tests and the Irish resolution which was against the spread of nuclear weapons, and holding over the debate on all the disarmament resolutions except the Canadian until March 7. The Indian delegation moved an amendment to include the Canadian resolution along with the other nine.
This finally came to a vote; there was a strong attempt made to get us to forget about it and just agree to let it go over until March but we insisted upon its being brought to a vote. The final result was that 17 voted in favour of having the Canadian resolution voted upon at once; 29 voted against, including all the Soviet bloc and some of the African countries-26 abstained and 27 were absent. You can tell from this how many wanted to go home for Christmas without having to vote on any issue of this kind. However, this means the resolution will now come up again when the first committee resumes its sittings on March 7.
The unfortunate feature is that for the next two and a half or perhaps three months nothing will be done about disarmament. The nuclear weapons race will go on, and more destructive weapons will be invented. The whole disarmament issue will be dormant for that time, just as it has been dormant since June 27. I think perhaps some of the other nations do not feel the urgency about disarmament that we do. They hang back, therefore, waiting for the nuclear powers to make a move. In any event, it is difficult to get action in the United Nations. However, I would hope members of the house will not be impatient. As I have said, our resolutions will be up again in March. I hope we will have 35 co-sponsors by then. We will do our best.
In any event, the end result may be very good. It just may be possible to get this resolution through unanimously, or it may not. We may get defeated again. I cannot make any promises. Canada has been doing the best she can to get some action on this question of disarmament and I assure you, Mr. Speaker, we shall continue to do that.

I thank the minister for this correction, but he will not think me less appreciative, if I say that the resolution put forward in the name of Canada and co-sponsored by Norway and Sweden is essentially a resolution of a procedural kind. As a matter of fact, this was the very point taken yesterday in the United Nations by the minister's parliamentary secretary in taking issue with Mr. Krishna Menon, who had said the Canadian proposal was a substantive one. The minister's parliamentary secretary took the position that this was merely a resolution dealing with procedure, and therefore there should be no difficulty in the resolution receiving the accord which the Canadian government and its spokesmen hoped would be forthcoming. The very ground taken by Mr. Krishna Menon, the delegate for India, was as I mentioned, that this was a resolution dealing with a matter of substance in the field of disarmament.
In so far as the character of the resolution is concerned, everyone in this house I am sure will agree that Canada, one of the original members of the subcommittee on disarmament, should take a lead in trying to bring about some persuasive effect in the field of disarmament through association with countries of the middle power group or with countries who belong to another category. We, through the Leader of the Opposition, put forward this very proposal, if the Secretary of State for External Affairs will recall, when this matter of disarmament was discussed in this house last winter.
However, the proposal Canada now has before the United Nations is not of the same

order as that proposed by the Leader of the Opposition. We should like to see Canada not only take an initiative in the matter of procedural formulae for disarmament but in putting forward a proposal of substance itself. Such a proposal might have an effect in persuading countries like the Scandinavian group, about which my hon. friend spoke so appreciatively and with justification. It might receive the support of other countries such as Brazil and Mexico. In any event, we would hope that between now and March it may be possible for the government to give consideration to strengthening its initiative at the United Nations not only by proposing an improvement in the matter of procedure but also in the matter of a substantial proposition which might be considered by the great powers in particular.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, may I say this. The minister has mentioned the fact that this matter will again come up for consideration on March 7. He has said that nothing can be done in the field of disarmament until that time. I would point out to him that there is no reason now, as far as I am aware, why the 10-power committee itself could not be reconvened at any time before March 7. If that were to happen, I am sure the minister would be among the first to applaud whatever initiative would be taken by any country toward the realization of that objective.
That being the case, and as Canada is a member of the 10-power committee, I take advantage of this opportunity to suggest to the minister that he might give consideration, once again, outside of the United Nations, before the resumption of the assembly meeting, to an initiative that might bring about a resumption of the 10-power meeting. If the minister could succeed in doing that he would win the gratitude of this country and of the people of the world.

Mr. Speaker, I have given careful thought to the question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Essex East, that the house be advised, concerning the 17 permits, of the dates of the permits and of the types and quantities of goods covered in each case, with regard to shipments to Cuba.
I have to bear in mind the undertaking which is given to applicants for export permits that the details they disclose will be treated as confidential. I also have to bear in mind the very important principle observed in the Statistics Act, namely that if there are less: than three exporters of any one category of

Inquiries of the Ministry goods, statistics of export trade will not be separately disclosed but combined with those of other statistical items.
This principle is equally important as it affects disclosure of information on use of export permits, and would be involved in this case in connection with several of these permits. The information which has been requested, coupled with what will shortly appear in the trade statistics, could very well give to anyone knowledgeable in the trades concerned some commercial intelligence useful to potential competitors of the exporters, not only those within Canada but also their competitors in foreign countries. This would provide just the sort of commercial intelligence for which foreign competition is always on the lookout. Unfortunately it is impossible to predict in advance where damage of this nature can occur, and it is certainly in the public interest that the details of the business of Canadian exporters facing competition in foreign markets should be safeguarded.
As I explained in my statement to the house on Friday, December 16, I would have no reason to refuse the tabling of these permits if it were not for this important matter of principle, and I also explained that in disclosing the information I then gave the house I was already going further than I would in normal circumstances consider appropriate.

I have decided that it is time to call a halt to further public disclosure of the details of these transactions. Each successive disclosure represents a further impairment of the assurance of confidential treatment given to applicants. As I reminded the house the other day, it has been the consistent practice of this government, and of the preceding government, to respect the confidential nature of the information which must be disclosed by firms applying for export permits, and we do not intend to depart from this practice.

We believe the time has come in Canada to build a new society with new ideas, a new sense of values and a new purpose. The United States way of life has become a shoddy thing to large sections of the world, and it is time we began to build a Canadian way of life as an independent nation.

Until this year, Mr. Chairman, only two municipalities and those the largest two, the city of Niagara Falls and the township of Stamford, with which I was associated, participated at all in the federal-provincial-municipal winter works incentive program. This year there is more participation and I will deal in particular with some of these types of projects as I go along.
There have been certain members of the house, Mr. Chairman, who have said that the riding of Niagara Falls was not a depressed area and they referred to newspaper articles to support their position. However, the Minister of Labour knows that this is not the case. Within the past two months he has been in the riding of Niagara Falls, as has the Minister of Defence Production. I should like to refer particularly to some remarks made by the Minister of Labour on that occasion when he visited the town of Fort Erie which is in the southern part of the riding of Niagara Falls. He was quoted in the Niagara Falls Review of October 21 as having said the following:
When the employment of 300 people In a town like Fort Erie is at stake we in Ottawa are very concerned. I can assure you-
He was speaking, of course, to a political meeting.
-we are looking into the matter very closely and more contracts will be forthcoming.
This was a reference to certain contracts which had been let fortuitously during the month of October by the Department of Defence Production to an aircraft plant in Fort Erie. I continue to quote:
The minister said: "When Raymond O'Hurley, the Minister of Defence Production, returned to Ottawa-

He had been in Niagara Falls just before that.
-I spoke to him and asked him what the situation was here. 'Mike', he answered, 'I will have to find something more for those people in Fort Erie because we simply must keep them in work.' "

Mr. Starr added:	"And I believe Raymond

I suggest that this indicates that at least in October of this year the Minister of Labour knew that in the riding of Niagara Falls there was cause for some concern over the increasing unemployment. I have before me certain figures which are as up to date as I was able to obtain dealing with Niagara and particularly the town of Fort Erie. These figures are weekly, commencing with October 10, 1960, and are taken up to December 9, 1960. Those unemployed in the week ending November 10 were 552 in number, including men and women, whereas at the same time in 1959 there were 438. In the week ending December 9, 1960 there were 866, an increase of 57 per cent in one month's time, whereas there had been 776 a year earlier. I do not have the figures as yet for December 20, but it is indicated there has been a rise of between 50 and 100 people every week in the last five weeks. It is apparent also that there will be approximately 1,000 people unemployed in Fort Erie now.
In so far as the Niagara Falls area is concerned, I have the monthly figures taken from the official figures of the unemployment insurance office there. However, I am able to contrast these figures for every month from 1956 to the month of November, 1960 inclusive. I should like to read these into the record to bring to the attention of the Minister of Labour what is happening in this area. I have taken them from the month of October to the month of April, inclusive, these being the months when the winter works program is applicable.
In 1956, during the month of October, there were 456 people out of work; in November, 617; in December, 1,317; in January, 1957, 1,738 people out of work; in February, 2,266; in March, 2,365 and in April, 2,023. It will be noted, Mr. Chairman, that this was the last year of the Liberal administration. In October, 1959 there were 1,145 people out of work in Niagara Falls, three times the number for the same month of 1956; in November, 1959 there were 1,581; in December, 2,528, twice as many as in the same month in 1956; in January, 1960 the figure leaped to 3,418, more than double the number for the same month of 1956; in February, 1960 3,460; in March, 3,304, and in April, 3,097. In October, 1960, there were 1,443 people

out of work and in November, 2,071. It is apparent that the December figure will be close to 3,000. There will be about 4,000 men and women unemployed in the Niagara Falls riding by the time I return to that riding tomorrow.
We have been listening to the preparations made by this government to put these Canadians, and individuals like them across this great nation, back to work. We have been unable to obtain any information from the Minister of Labour as to what immediate prospects these people have of finding employment. The only proviso is that there is in the supplementary estimates an additional sum of $30 million for winter works. The winter works program was broadened this year to some extent and considerable publicity was given to the fact it was announced earlier. But it is apparent, Mr. Chairman, that those who announced this program and designed it know little about municipal life and little about the timing in which the municipalities prepare their budgets. I would assume that there are those in this government who had municipal experience earlier and know that the municipalities strike their budgets early in the year.
When money has to be raised by a municipality for its portion, which is far greater than the portion this government pays for any winter works project, it has to be obtained in one of two ways, either paid for at once, in which case it becomes a part of the general rate against real property in the municipality, or else borrowed by debentures. It cannot be argued by any member of the government that raising money by debentures is not extremely expensive, particularly in the last three years during the regime of this government, and it has finally reached the point where many municipalities cannot afford to borrow at all.
When the budget is struck in March, the municipalities must then arrange what their spending is to be. They are unable to prepare, at that time, for a surplus. It is their responsibility, just as it is this government's, to keep their general rate to the lowest possible level. Thus when the government comes along and announces in August or September, that it is to start a new winter works program in October it is virtually of no benefit to any municipality in the province of Ontario, unless it be a municipality with a surplus on hand and that is something that does not exist any more or unless it be a municipality that is able to raise money by debentures.
Of the seven municipalities in the riding of Niagara Falls, all but one are required to debenture, and each of those municipalities has almost reached the point where the Ontario municipal board will not permit them

to borrow further. I should like to point out that in an area such as the city of Niagara Falls, which has been facing great capital expenditures and which will have in the next year or so a very large capital expenditure for sewage and filtration plants which it cannot afford, in the year 1959-60 they applied and received approval for certain projects under this government's proposals which required them to spend $110,000. There was a total subsidy from this and the provincial government of somewhat less than $12,000. It was necessary, therefore, to spend almost $100,000 in order to benefit from this magnificent winter works program.
In each of the municipalities the same sort of payment is required to be made. In the township of Stamford this year $162,800 will have to be spent in order to obtain a subsidy from both governments of a little over $50,000. The village of Chippewa, where for the first time they are able to construct a badly needed firehall and municipal building, has gone out and raised money for this building and is able to obtain a subsidy of only $20,000. This is for a public utility. The rest of the money must be raised by debentures.
Now, Mr. Chairman, if you raise money by debentures, it is paid for in exactly the same way as money which is in the general rate, that is the taxpayer who owns his property pays for it. This is nothing short of welfare, and this government has shifted the welfare from the shoulders of the whole of the people of Canada, a principle which under the Liberal administration was well accepted, and put it on the shoulders of the person who owns real property.
I suggest to this government that this is no! the place for this type of work. If all the work that was to be done under winter works was of a capital nature, something which would increase the stake in the community, I would suggest it might be more acceptable. However, when this government, under its leader, recommends that money be spent on such things as clearing brush, which seems to be something about which hon. gentlemen opposite are becoming experts, something which can be of no real benefit in the future, rather than on such things as constructing water filtration plants, something of real use in the future, then there is no justification for imposing this burden on the owners of real property.
I have sent out a survey and have asked each of the municipalities in what way such a program as this might be strengthened. In the first place it is suggested and has been approved by the Ontario municipal association-and these recommendations have been sent to this government but have received the

usual kind of consideration-that the subsidies paid by this government cover not just the cost of raw labour but also the cost of material and overhead. There is no question that if material be purchased for use in a winter works program, this procedure also creates jobs which create more jobs. The present figures are indicating that well above 50 per cent in most cases must be spent by the municipalities on such things as materials. Particularly if you get into such things as sewage or water pipes or anything of that kind, the greatest cost is, of course, in material.
It is also suggested that the government pay subsidies on the wages of regular staff which are assigned to winter works. In such municipalities as those which have permanent engineering staffs or which have foremen which are taken off regular maintenance work and sent out on this work, the municipality is of course paying them and is not receiving the subsidies from the provincial department of highways.
It is further suggested-and this is one of the more important things the minister may consider-that there be interim payment of subsidies. As the situation now is municipalities are having to borrow money or to go into overdraft or find the money wherever they can in order to keep their people working and they are not paid for about ten months. Most municipalities cannot afford this, particularly if it is a large expenditure in relation to their annual budget. It is therefore suggested that the government might consider making interim payments of these subsidies. Since the work must be completed by the end of April surely there seems to be no reason why payments may not be made from time to time.
I suggested earlier in my remarks that the government deal with the program of the following year. It is apparent from year to year during this government's life that unemployment is becoming an increasing problem across Canada. It is an unhappy thing. It is not a thing for anyone to gloat over. It is not a thing for anyone to be happy about. It is not just the hon. member for St. James who spoke a few moments ago who is concerned about those who come to his office to beg for work. These people are now losing what under 22 years of good government they were able to build up. I refer to their cars and their homes.
Oh, oh.
I am surprised that hon. gentlemen should be so pleased. Since they are sitting here, being sure of an indemnity of a type, they at least are not unemployed.

Shame.

They should be concerned for those across Canada who are unemployed.
She gives only what she has; she cannot give what she does not possess.

I should be pleased to give whatever of my substance I have in order to assist these people. However, it is a real problem today because they are unable to keep up the payments; they are unable to retain what they have. These people want to work. In many cases they have gone to the municipalities to ask for an opportunity to work. The municipalities have been obliged to say, "We cannot take you on; we can take only people whose benefits are gone". Hence even those who wish to go off unemployment insurance and to be gainfully employed are not at liberty to do so. The municipalities in my riding have had to take those who are in real need, whose employment benefits have been long gone.
These projects which have been set up will not employ more than 123 people in the whole of Niagara Falls riding which has approximately 4,000 unemployed.
That is the standard all over the country.

I have had figures given to me and in some cases they indicate that as many as 90 will be employed. Yet the works manager or the engineer of the city I understand says in each case, "Pay no attention to the 90 men". I wonder about the figures used by the Minister of Labour when he tells us how many men are to be employed in each province as he did yesterday in answer to the hon. member for Essex East. For instance, in the case of the city of Niagara Falls, under their approval it was indicated that 90 men would be employed. I should like to quote from a letter which I received from the city manager of that city. He states as follows:
The total number of men to be employed as shown on the program for 1960-61 is misleading because we will never have anything like 90 men on the job at one time and many of the men employed will be moved from one job to another.
I would estimate that we will not exceed 30 men on the work staff at any time. This is only a very small proportion of men that require work during the winter months.
There are 123 men who will be employed in Niagara Falls and these will be employed for different periods of time. When the government produces figures it does not indicate whether an individual man is to be employed for a day or for three or four months; nor do the projects themselves indicate their duration. I suggest to the minister that the figures are just false and misleading to the people of Canada.

May I interrupt the hon. lady if she will allow me to do so in order to get this matter straightened out. As to these figures as to the number of men to be employed, I am afraid the hon. member will have to apply to the officials of Niagara Falls because they supplied us with those figures.

The engineer for the township of Stamford reported that a subsidy on materials could double winter works. On

the Stamford winter works program for this year, which is the largest one in the whole riding of Niagara Falls, it is estimated that 45 men will there be employed for 44,256 hours.
There is nothing, I suggest also, which leads this government to recommend even to the municipalities what hourly rate will be paid to employees. In some municipalities employees are paid well below prevailing rates and well below prevailing rates in construction. I have been informed that this is a memorable occasion for the hon. member for Niagara Falls. Not only has she just done a little bit more than hold her own with the Minister of Labour in the exchange that has just taken place but it is also the occasion of her birthday, and I congratulate her.

We are dealing with the government's program to provide winter works, and certainly a winter works program is greatly needed in this country at this time. It is not only needed because of the normal seasonal type of unemployment; it is needed because of greatly increased unemployment at this time, further aggravated by regional unemployment, concentrated as it is to quite an extent in the Atlantic provinces. Therefore the government's proposals are most important in relation to this all-embracing problem.

I have in my hand a publication by the economics and research branch of the Department of Labour, Canada, 1960, entitled "Seasonal Unemployment in Canada". It contains a wealth of information on this very serious problem. For example, in a table on page 21 it points out the vast increases in unemployment, the percentage increase from summer to winter; the average from 1954 to
1959	in unemployment of certain skilled workers in the construction industry. For example, bricklayers and tilesetters show an increase of 1,002.8 per cent; plasterers, an increase of 1,165.6 per cent.
Therefore it is not just a question of training people and expecting that as a result of their training will come job opportunities, because certainly in the construction industry the people who are skilled are just as much unemployed in the winter time as the ordinary workers in that industry. But this is the government's answer, along with certain other legislation, to this serious unemployment problem, aggravated as it is by a seasonal factor.
I have in my hand certain information that has been provided by the minister's department. It is a projection of the number of men to be hired in the period October 15,
1960	to April 30, 1961 as a result of the government's winter works project. It contains some very excellent information in that it enables members of the committee to judge just how comprehensive is the government's program, and allows members of the committee to decide, with the facts available, just how far short the government's program comes to picking up what might be termed the normal increase in unemployment because of the seasonal factor.
The publication to which I have already referred contains this statement on page 12, and I wish to quote it. It points out the extent of the seasonal unemployment problem when it states:
It is estimated that under reasonably full employment conditions, and with a labour force of about six million-[DOT]
Now over six million:
-some 250,000 persons-about 4 per cent of the labour force-are seasonally unemployed at midwinter. This figure may be slightly larger when employment is declining and slightly smaller when employment is expanding, as the seasonal amplitude appears to be affected in some indeterminate way both by changes in job opportunities and the level of total unemployment.
In general the amount of seasonal unemployment at mid-winter is declared to be 4 per cent of the labour force of Canada. As it is at the present time with the working force at the present level it amounts to some 250,000 persons.

The government's projected employment as a result of the winter works program is that 78,627 persons will be hired and that they will have in total some 3,597,320 man-days of work. The minister has just said 40, but my calculation is that this will amount to 46 working days per man placed on the job. Yet if one calculates the actual number of working days, excluding week ends and holidays, from October 15 to April 30 there are 138 working days. Yet every person who obtains employment under this program gets only 46 working days.
Therefore, even those who are employed are idle for two thirds of the time. This is really not an adequate winter works program. Even those who are successful enough to obtain work under the program will be idle two thirds of the time from October 15 until April 30. If one calculates the number of persons who receive employment on the average for 138 working days in this period, then this is a program that provides winter work over this period of time for just over 26,000 persons. Yet according to the government's own publication the seasonal unemployment in Canada amounts to 250,000. This is apart altogether from the abnormally high unemployment in the country today over and above the seasonal factor. Those persons provided with jobs for the winter period under this program amount to 26,000-just over 26,000-and yet the number of persons who are seasonally unemployed amounts to 250,000.
In other words, this program, valuable as it is, after all the blaring of trumpets and all the fanfare that the government has arranged in connection with its operation, is just 10 per cent effective when it comes to putting the seasonally unemployed to work, to say nothing of putting the vast numbers of unemployed to work who are in excess of the seasonal workers.
Would the hon. member permit a question? On what does the hon. member base his 10 per cent figure?

I base it on the statistics I hold in my hand from the Department of Labour and on the booklet from which the hon. member would know I had quoted, if the hon. member had been in his place, entitled "Seasonal unemployment in Canada, Economics and research branch, Department of Labour, Canada, 1960".
These figures are taken from official publications; my statistics are taken from the government's own figures. The calculations I have made are based on those statistics. I suggest that the government's program, valuable as it is, welcome as it is, helpful as it is, is just 10 per cent effective in dealing with this vast unemployment problem.

The government, the minister and his colleagues will have to present to parliament in other legislation and in other ways a tar greater program, a tar more effective program to deal with unemployment, and in particular to deal with seasonal unemployment, than the government has presented in this feeble, ineffective, 10 per cent program which we have been discussing today and last night.

I do not intend to hold up this committee and I am not going to repeat what has been so ably said by the hon. lady member for Niagara Falls and the hon. member for Assiniboia about the inadequacy of the program, but I cannot allow this vote to go by without repeating what we have said on this side of the house, and particularly what hon. members representing the Atlantic provinces on this side of the house have said about the inequitable character of this program-the fact that this program favours those municipalities which are the richest and which have the least unemployment and discriminates against those which have the least resources and the most unemployment. This follows by definition because the same 50 per cent formula is applied to all of them.
Some of us did think that when the government decided to include unemployment among the topics which were to come before the federal-provincial conference last October, perhaps it was willing to listen to some of the things that were said. Last night the hon. member for Laurier put on record in Hansard what was said by the premier of Quebec, the Hon. Jean Lesage, who during the course of that conference took substantially the same position as has been taken by the Liberal opposition here, namely that the contribution should be on a sliding scale; that it should be higher in those areas where there was heavy unemployment and in those areas where there was small ability to pay. Mr. Lesage pointed out as was pointed out by the hon. lady this afternoon that a very large part of these costs is not for direct labour on the spot but for materials and for that reason many municipalities are inhibited from taking part in the program.
But instead of listening to the constructive suggestions made by the premier of Quebec, what was the attitude of the government when that conference was over? I think we ought to have on the permanent record of parliament the Minister of Labour's own estimate of that conference, because I think it has not received enough publicity, and I think it will shock the people of this country to hear it. I have taken the minister's comments from the local organ of his party, the Ottawa Journal, a report by Mr. Richard Jackson who does not go out of his way to

report unfavourably on the present government. This is from the Ottawa Journal of October 29, 1960 and the headline reads: "Everybody Unhappy. Conference Nowhere on Tax Deal, Jobless." I am not going to read anything about the tax deal, Mr. Chairman. The article points out that the conference got nowhere in connection with this matter, and then it goes on to say:
Even more bleak had been the performance of the conference on unemployment.
"Out of it came not one single useful idea," confessed Labour Minister Starr.
"The premiers were the ones who insisted on talking about unemployment.-
In other words, the federal government was not even sufficiently interested to put this question on the agenda until it was asked to do so. The premiers were the ones who wanted to talk about unemployment. The quotation continues:
-and so we rather expected they might have some helpful suggestions. They had none that could be applied on a national basis. Each had his own provincial axe to grind, each his own provincial project to push."
The Charlottetown Guardian, also a supporter of the present government, quoted the minister as saying, on the same day, October 29:
"There were no suggestions today from any of the provinces for any national project. Each province had its own axe to grind, some particular project like the Chignecto canal in New Brunswick."
Since the leader of the party opposite, the Prime Minister himself, had promised to build the Chignecto canal, did the Minister of Labour expect the premier of New Brunswick to say nothing about it? The thing that is so extraordinary is that here was a national conference of all the premiers, dealing with a problem whose importance the government should have recognized, and one might have thought that some attention would have been paid to the constructive ideas and advice which were forthcoming from at least one provincial premier, as the hon. member for Laurier pointed out last night. Instead they complained because the provinces did not provide a national solution.
How absurd can you be? Provincial governments are elected to look after the affairs of their provinces and they would not be doing their duty properly if they did not look after those affairs. The government of Canada is returned to look after national affairs, and if this unemployment is not a national problem, then we have no national problem today. It is far and away our greatest problem.
As I have said, I do not intend to hold up this item, but I do want to point out again that this program is not only inadequate, as the hon. member for Niagara Falls and others

have said, but that it is also inequitable. If the government had accepted at least the suggestion made by the premier of Quebec for a more equitable distribution of the costs of the winter works program to the federal treasury there would have been the possibility of much greater participation in areas such as eastern Quebec and the Atlantic provinces where unemployment is relatively most serious and where ability to pay is least.
My attention has been drawn to an item which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen on December 14-a little squib which is very relevant to what we are discussing now- which reads:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker has said that his government's first three and a half years in office have been spent clearing the underbrush.
So that is what the government has been up to. A lot of people have been thinking it was lost in the woods.
As far as this problem of unemployment is concerned it is perfectly evident that this statement is an accurate assumption.

I have one or two suggestions to make to the restaurant committee on behalf of this group. First of all, we believe that the restaurant committee should give consideration to the restoration of the principle and practice of seniority with respect to waitresses in the restaurant. The second complaint I wish to make has to do with the menus. We understand that the chef receives a very good salary, I am told $500 a month, and that during the time the house is not in session he goes on vacation. I believe our House of Commons restaurant should provide Canadian meals representative of Canadian menus, and I suggest that the restaurant committee give consideration to allowing the chef to spend some time during his holidays as an observer in the lumbering and mining camps of British Columbia so that he will understand what good Canadian meals are. I say that because I think you have to have that experience to understand the type of meals that Canadians like. Mr. Chairman, I think I can do no better than simply set out the general field and ambit of the commission. It will report upon steps that may be taken to eliminate duplication and overlapping of services, to eliminate unnecessary or uneconomic operations, and generally the achieving of efficiency or economy through further decentralization of operations and administration.
To sum up, the purposes of the commission are to achieve efficiency or economy through reallocation or regrouping of units of the public service, to make more effective use of budgeting, accounting and other financial measures as a means of achieving more efficient and economical management of departments and agencies; improving efficiency and economy by alterations in the relations between government departments and agencies, on the one hand, and treasury board and other central control or service agencies of the government, on the other. subtopic: MR. HOWARD    ELIGIBILITY OF MINISTERS TO SIT IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
MR. HOWARD    ELIGIBILITY OF MINISTERS TO SIT IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I rise on a question of privilege. I rise at this time because of the urgency, importance and appropriateness that I, personally, feel it must be dealt with at this time. This question of privilege concerns the house and every member in it, and more particularly the members of the cabinet. My question of privilege is that some, if not all, members of the cabinet are not eligible to sit or vote in the House of Commons because of the provisions of section 10 of the Senate and House of Commons Act, which section provides that no person accepting any employment in the service of the government of Canada to which any emolument is attached is eligible as a member of the House of Commons, or shall sit or vote therein. Some, if not all, of the members of the cabinet have accepted such emoluments specifically, all or part of the $2,000 annual motorcar allowance.
Perhaps in explanation of this I could refer to the public accounts of Canada for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1959, volume 1, where

Question of Privilege
at page K6 is indicated, for instance, that the Minister cd Finance (Mr. Fleming) received such a $2,000 motorcar allowance pursuant to the Appropriation Act No. 5, being chapter 61 of the statutes of 1931. I would point out that the Appropriation Act No. 5 at one time gave statutory exemption from the provisions of section 10 of the Senate and House of Commons Act, in that a vote No. 352 contained in schedule A of the said Appropriation Act No. 5 provides as follows, and I quote from that schedule as shown on page 465 of the Statutes of Canada for 1931:
-for payment annually from the consolidated revenue fund of the sum of $2,000 to each minister of the crown charged with the administration of a department, the Solicitor General, and the Leader of the Opposition, and the sum of $1,000 each to the Speaker of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Commons, in lieu of motorcars and their maintenance, including chauffeurs, the acceptance of such sums not to vacate their respective seats in parliament:-
The last part is the saving feature of that vote. This statutory vote had effect only until the fifteenth day of September, 1953, and I should explain that this statutory protection no longer exists by virtue of chapter 67 of the 1948 statutes, being an Act respecting the Revised Statutes of Canada, under which a commission was established to revise the public general statutes of Canada. The commission was authorized to append a schedule to the revision and to include in the schedule, and I quote from section 4 of the 1948 statutes:
-all acts and parts of acts which though not expressly repealed, are superseded by the acts so consolidated, or are inconsistent therewith, and all acts and parts of acts which were for a temporary purpose, the force of which is spent.

That Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in previous budget speeches and on other occasions I have recognized the need for flexibility in our economic 90205-6-64
The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming policies. Last March, when presenting the budget to this house, I stated that "sound budget policies must be flexible and adapted to changing economic conditions". Not only must policies be flexible from year to year, but there are occasions when it becomes appropriate to reassess the economic outlook and to adjust fiscal policies between the main budget dates. This is such a time. (Translation):
Supplementary budgets are not entirely novel in the Canadian experience. They are intended to deal with important changes in the situation that may emerge within the course of the year. A responsible government cannot stand by and allow events to take their course simply on the ground that budgets are brought down only once a year. This government will continue to maintain flexibility in its fiscal and other policies to meet the needs of the Canadian people.
The introduction of a supplementary budget for the current fiscal year will not take the place of the presentation of a regular budget for the next fiscal year. Before the current year's budget is presented there will be the usual careful review of the tax structure with full consideration of the various suggestions for adjustments and technical changes which have been received during the year.
The need for a supplementary budget at this time arises from a number of recent developments. While some of them originated in Canada, most of them originated abroad and it is to the latter that I shall address myself first.
